```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.4)
```

```{r}
library(rbfkernel)
```

The RBF (Gaussian) kernel turns distance into similarity:
$K(x, x') = \exp(-\gamma \lVert x - x' \rVert^2)$. Models built on it can fit
curved relationships and boundaries. Two settings matter: the **width**
$\gamma$ and the **regularisation** $\lambda$ (or the SVM cost $C$).
`rbfkernel` tunes both for you.

## 1. One call on any data frame

Give `rbf_workflow()` a data frame and the column to predict:

```{r}
wf <- rbf_workflow(breast_cancer, target = "diagnosis")
wf
```

It used the other 30 columns as features, standardised them on the training
rows only, tuned $\gamma$ and $\lambda$ by **exact leave-one-out**, and scored
the tuned model on 142 rows it never saw. Because the classes are imbalanced,
it tuned for balanced accuracy.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3}
plot(wf)
```

The heat map shows leave-one-out performance over the grid (the red cross is
the choice). Large $\gamma$ with small $\lambda$ overfits; small $\gamma$ with
large $\lambda$ underfits.

Use the tuned model on new rows. Encoding and scaling are applied
automatically:

```{r}
predict(wf, breast_cancer[c(1, 100, 300), ])
```

## 2. Other kinds of data

**Multiclass**, with a stratified split:

```{r}
rbf_workflow(iris, "Species", plot = FALSE)$confusion
```

**Regression** with a categorical feature (one-hot encoded automatically),
compared with a predict-the-mean baseline:

```{r}
cars <- transform(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp", "cyl")], cyl = factor(cyl))
w <- rbf_workflow(cars, "mpg", plot = FALSE)
w$metrics
w$baseline
```

**Missing values** are dropped and reported:

```{r}
rbf_workflow(airquality[, 1:4], "Ozone", plot = FALSE)$notes
```

**Two features**: the figure adds the decision regions:

```{r}
moons <- make_moons(300, noise = 0.25)
plot(rbf_workflow(moons, "class", plot = FALSE))
```

**An SVM instead of kernel ridge** (needs the e1071 package), tuned by 5-fold
cross-validation with scaling inside each fold:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("e1071", quietly = TRUE)}
rbf_workflow(breast_cancer, "diagnosis", method = "svm", plot = FALSE)$metrics
```

Set `output_dir` to save the metrics, tuning grid, test predictions, confusion
matrix, figure and a text report.

## 3. Why tuning is fast: exact leave-one-out

For kernel ridge, the leave-one-out residual has a closed form,
$e_i = \alpha_i / [(K + \lambda I)^{-1}]_{ii}$. With one eigendecomposition
$K = U D U^\top$ per $\gamma$, every $\lambda$ costs only matrix products:

```{r}
tuned <- krr_tune(iris[, 1:4], iris$Species, lambdas = 10^seq(-4, 2, by = 0.5))
tuned
nrow(tuned$grid)   # (gamma, lambda) pairs, each an exact leave-one-out score
```

## 4. Building blocks

```{r}
x <- scale(as.matrix(iris[, 1:4]))
c(scale = gamma_scale(x), median = gamma_median(x))   # starting values for gamma
K <- rbf_kernel(x, gamma = 0.25)
fit <- krr(iris[, 1:4], iris$Species, gamma = 0.25, lambda = 0.1)
head(predict(fit, iris[, 1:4], type = "score"), 3)
```

For large data, replace the n x n kernel by an explicit feature map and use a
linear model on it:

```{r}
Zr <- predict(rff_map(x, 0.25, n_components = 2000), x)   # random Fourier features
Zn <- predict(nystroem_map(x, 0.25, n_components = 50), x) # Nystroem, 50 landmarks
c(rff = max(abs(tcrossprod(Zr) - K)), nystroem = max(abs(tcrossprod(Zn) - K)))
```
